title: ggplot2 Hands-On Practice
text:
Activity 1: Fill in the blanks
Goal: Build a scatterplot of penguin bill length vs. bill depth, colored by species, using what you learned today.
Instructions: Fill in the ___ blanks to complete the code. Run it and check that your plot displays correctly!

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Bill length and bill depth by species",
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(h = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(h = 0.5)
  )

Hints:

The dataset you’ve been using all day goes in the first blank
Find the variable name for bill depth
Use the same geom as the scatterplots in the presentation
Axis labels should be human-readable (e.g., “Bill depth (mm)”)
Revist Manually modifying theme slides to center titles

Bonus: Can you also add shape = species inside aes() to make the plot accessible to colorblind viewers?

title: ggplot2 Hands-On Practice
text:
Activity 2: Update the facet plots
Goal: Recreate and then enhance the faceted penguin plot from the presentation.
Instructions: Start with the faceted plot from the slides, then make the following modifications:

Apply a theme — add a theme with the following specifications:


Position the title and subtitle to be right aligned
Set the legend position to “bottom”
Remove major and minor gridlines
Add axes lines that are colored blue
Set your theme as a function before applying it to your figure.


Add color — map color = species inside so each species panel has a distinct color
Fix the legend position — the default legend.position = c(0.85, 0.2) may overlap the facets; adjust it to "bottom" instead Bonus: Try facet_grid(sex ~ species) instead of facet_wrap(~ species). What changes? What does this tell you that the original plot didn’t?


# Facet plots from presentation - modify according to instructions above
mytheme <- ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 1, face = "bold"), # hor. adjust title to center
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 1, face = "bold"), # hor. adjust subtitle to center
    legend.position = "bottom", # x, y from bottom-left corner on scale 0-1
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "blue")
  )


ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)
) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin body mass by flipper length",
    subtitle = "Faceted by species",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)",
    color = "species"
  ) +
  mytheme

Goal: Use the mtcars dataset to independently apply everything from the presentation to answer a research question.
Background: mtcars is a built-in R dataset containing performance and design specs for 32 car models. Run ?mtcars to see the full variable list. Key variables:



Variable
Description




mpg
Miles per gallon


hp
Horsepower


wt
Weight (1000 lbs)


cyl
Number of cylinders (4, 6, or 8)


am
Transmission (0 = automatic, 1 = manual)



Research question: Does the relationship between horsepower and fuel efficiency differ by number of cylinders?
Your task — build a complete, publication-ready figure that:

Plots horsepower (x) vs. mpg (y) as a scatterplot

Applies a clean custom theme

Write Your Own Visualization Function
In this exercise, you will create a reusable function that produces a scatterplot using ggplot2. Your function should allow the user to choose the dataset, the variables to plot, and any optional arguments supported by ggplot2::geom_point().
Step 1
Create a function named custom_visualization() with four arguments:

data: the data frame to plot.
xvar: the variable to display on the x-axis.
yvar: the variable to display on the y-axis.
… additional arguments that will be passed directly to ggplot2::geom_point().

Step 2
Before creating the plot, remove any rows where both the x and y variables are missing (NA).

Use dplyr::filter().
Inside filter(), use dplyr::if_any().
Use embracing ({{ }}) so that the function accepts unquoted variable names.
The condition should only keep rows that do not have an NA.

Hint: The expression inside if_any() should refer to the range from xvar to yvar, and the predicate should be is.na.
Step 3
Pipe the filtered data into ggplot2::ggplot().
Use ggplot2::aes() to map:

x to xvar
y to yvar
Remember to use embracing ({{ }}) for both variables.

Step 4
Add a scatterplot layer using ggplot2::geom_point().
Instead of specifying arguments like color or size yourself, forward all optional arguments using .... This allows users to customize the points by passing any arguments accepted by geom_point(), such as: color, size, shape, fill, alpha, stroke, etc.
Step 5
Test your function using the filtered_flights data frame. Create a scatterplot of:

temp on the x-axis
wind_speed on the y-axis

Customize the points by passing several optional arguments through …, for example:
color = “blue” size = 4 shape = 21 stroke = 2 fill = “red”
If your function is written correctly, these arguments should be passed automatically to ggplot2::geom_point() without modifying the function itself.

title: Subsetting in R
text:
Activity 1: [, [[, and $

Why three operators?
R gives you three tools for pulling things out of an object, and they are not interchangeable:








Operator
What it returns
Typical use




[
A subset of the same type/structure (can hold 0, 1, or many elements)
“Give me a smaller version of this object”


[[
A single element, unwrapped from its container
“Give me the contents of this one slot”


$
A single named element (shorthand for [[ with a name)
“Give me the column/element called ___”



A helpful mental picture from Advanced R (Wickham): if a list is a train, and each element is a train car, then:

x[4:6] gives you a smaller train made of cars 4 through 6 (still a train — a list)
x[[5]] opens car 5 and hands you what’s inside it (not a train anymore)

This is why [ on a list always returns a list (even a list of length 1), while [[ and $ reach inside and hand you the actual object stored there.
Our parent_info column is a list-column — each element of kids$parent_info is itself a list. It’s a good place to see [ vs [[ vs $ in action.


Step 1: Look at the list-column

kids$parent_info



Step 2: Extract one child’s parent information
Suppose we want the parent information for child 3.

# Use [ ] to extract the third element of parent_info

# Now use [[ ]] to extract the same element

# Compare the classes of the two results

What’s different? [ keeps the “train car” wrapper — you get a list containing one list. [[ unwraps it and gives you the list itself. This is the simplify vs. preserve distinction: [[ simplifies (drops a layer of structure), [ preserves it.


Step 3: Extract information within the list
Now that we have the parent information for child 3, we want to extract just the mother’s name. Because parent_info[[3]] is a named list, we can use $ to grab a named piece of it.

# Extract the mother's name for child 3

The key idea: these operators chain together to walk through nested objects — first [[ to get into the list-column, then $ to get the named element inside.

title: Subsetting in R
text:
Activity 2: Selecting Rows and Columns
Data frames behave like a cross between a list (each column is an element) and a matrix (rows and columns). When subsetting with two indices, the pattern is:
data[rows, columns]

The first position (before the comma) says which rows
The second position (after the comma) says which columns
Leaving a position blank means “give me all of them”


# All columns for child 5
kids[5, ]

# The mvpa_min column, for all children
kids[, "mvpa_min"]


Your turn
Imagine you are preparing a small table for a research meeting. You want information for children 2, 5, 8, and 12 — but only the columns id, age, sex, mvpa_min, and vo2peak.

# Select children 2, 5, 8, and 12
# and keep only id, age, sex, mvpa_min, and vo2peak



Simplify vs. preserve: one more thing to notice
Compare these two approaches to grabbing a single column:

kids[, "mvpa_min"] # matrix-style: simplifies
kids["mvpa_min"] # list-style: preserves

They select the same values, but return different types of objects:

class(kids[, "mvpa_min"])
class(kids["mvpa_min"])

kids[, "mvpa_min"] simplifies down to a plain vector, because you asked for it “matrix style” (row, column). kids["mvpa_min"] treats kids like a list and hands you back a smaller data frame with one column, preserving the original structure. This distinction is a common source of bugs — a function that works fine when you select multiple columns can break unexpectedly when only one column is selected, because the object type silently changes. (Tibbles were designed to avoid this: kids[, "mvpa_min"] on a tibble still returns a tibble, not a bare vector — try it and compare to a base data.frame.)

title: Subsetting in R
text:
Activity 3: Logical Subsetting
So far we’ve selected rows by their position (row 5, rows 2/5/8/12). But in research data, we usually want to select rows by whether they meet a condition — “give me children who did X” rather than “give me row 7.”
This is where logical subsetting comes in. A logical condition like:

kids$mvpa_min >= 60

produces a vector of TRUE, FALSE, and possibly NA — one value per row. When you put that logical vector inside [, R keeps only the rows where the value is TRUE, and returns NA for rows where the condition itself was NA (this is different from using which(), which silently drops NAs instead — worth knowing when you’re not sure why your row counts don’t match).

Your turn
Find the children who get at least 60 minutes of MVPA. Return only id, age, mvpa_min, and vo2peak.

# Select children with at least 60 minutes of MVPA
# Keep only id, age, mvpa_min, and vo2peak



Try another one
Now find just the IDs of children who get less than 30 minutes of MVPA.

# Select the IDs of children with MVPA < 30

Notice this time you’re subsetting a vector (kids$id), not the whole data frame — same logical-subsetting idea, just applied outside the data[rows, columns] pattern.

title: Subsetting in R
text:
Activity 4: Combining Conditions
Multiple logical conditions can be combined with:



Operator
Meaning




&
AND (both conditions must be TRUE)


|
OR (at least one condition must be TRUE)


!
NOT (flips TRUE/FALSE)



Always use the vectorized & and | here (not && / ||, which only compare a single value each and are meant for if statements).

kids$mvpa_min >= 60 &
  kids$bmi_z < 1


Your turn
Identify children who have either low physical activity (MVPA < 30 minutes) or high BMI z-score (≥ 2). Return id, age, bmi_z, mvpa_min.

# Select children with either:
#   MVPA < 30
#   OR BMI z-score >= 2
#
# Keep id, age, bmi_z, and mvpa_min



Add another condition
Now restrict to girls who meet either of those criteria:

Female AND (low MVPA OR high BMI z-score)


# Select girls who either:
#   have MVPA < 30
#   OR have BMI z-score >= 2
#
# Keep id, age, sex, bmi_z, and mvpa_min

Why the parentheses matter: without them, R would evaluate & before | in a way that changes the meaning of the statement (operator precedence). The parentheses force the OR condition to be evaluated as a single unit before it’s combined with the AND. When in doubt, use parentheses to make your intent explicit — even when they’re not strictly required, they make code easier for you (and others) to read later.

Formula: miles = steps * 2.5 / 5280 (average stride length of 2.5 ft, 5,280 ft per mile)

title: Subsetting in R Solutions
text:
Activity 1: [, [[, and $

Why three operators?
R gives you three tools for pulling things out of an object, and they are not interchangeable:








Operator
What it returns
Typical use




[
A subset of the same type/structure (can hold 0, 1, or many elements)
“Give me a smaller version of this object”


[[
A single element, unwrapped from its container
“Give me the contents of this one slot”


$
A single named element (shorthand for [[ with a name)
“Give me the column/element called ___”



A helpful mental picture from Advanced R (Wickham): if a list is a train, and each element is a train car, then:

x[4:6] gives you a smaller train made of cars 4 through 6 (still a train — a list)
x[[5]] opens car 5 and hands you what’s inside it (not a train anymore)

This is why [ on a list always returns a list (even a list of length 1), while [[ and $ reach inside and hand you the actual object stored there.
Our parent_info column is a list-column — each element of kids$parent_info is itself a list. It’s a good place to see [ vs [[ vs $ in action.


Step 1: Look at the list-column

kids$parent_info



Step 2: Extract one child’s parent information
Suppose we want the parent information for child 3.

# [ ] extracts the third element as a length-1 list
kids$parent_info[3]

# [[ ]] extracts the third element itself (a named list, not wrapped in a list)
kids$parent_info[[3]]

class(kids$parent_info[3])
class(kids$parent_info[[3]])

What’s different? [ keeps the “train car” wrapper — you get a list containing one list. [[ unwraps it and gives you the list itself. This is the simplify vs. preserve distinction: [[ simplifies (drops a layer of structure), [ preserves it.


Step 3: Extract information within the list
Now that we have the parent information for child 3, we want to extract just the mother’s name. Because parent_info[[3]] is a named list, we can use $ to grab a named piece of it.

kids$parent_info[[3]]$mother

The key idea: these operators chain together to walk through nested objects — first [[ to get into the list-column, then $ to get the named element inside.

title: Subsetting in R Solutions
text:
Activity 2: Selecting Rows and Columns
Data frames behave like a cross between a list (each column is an element) and a matrix (rows and columns). When subsetting with two indices, the pattern is:
data[rows, columns]

The first position (before the comma) says which rows
The second position (after the comma) says which columns
Leaving a position blank means “give me all of them”


# All columns for child 5
kids[5, ]

# The mvpa_min column, for all children
kids[, "mvpa_min"]


Your turn
Imagine you are preparing a small table for a research meeting. You want information for children 2, 5, 8, and 12 — but only the columns id, age, sex, mvpa_min, and vo2peak.

# Select children 2, 5, 8, and 12
# and keep only id, age, sex, mvpa_min, and vo2peak

kids[
  c(2, 5, 8, 12),
  c("id", "age", "sex", "mvpa_min", "vo2peak")
]



Simplify vs. preserve: one more thing to notice
Compare these two approaches to grabbing a single column:

kids[, "mvpa_min"] # matrix-style: simplifies
kids["mvpa_min"] # list-style: preserves

They select the same values, but return different types of objects:

class(kids[, "mvpa_min"])
class(kids["mvpa_min"])

kids[, "mvpa_min"] simplifies down to a plain vector, because you asked for it “matrix style” (row, column). kids["mvpa_min"] treats kids like a list and hands you back a smaller data frame with one column, preserving the original structure. This distinction is a common source of bugs — a function that works fine when you select multiple columns can break unexpectedly when only one column is selected, because the object type silently changes. (Tibbles were designed to avoid this: kids[, "mvpa_min"] on a tibble still returns a tibble, not a bare vector — try it and compare to a base data.frame.)

title: Subsetting in R Solutions
text:
Activity 3: Logical Subsetting
So far we’ve selected rows by their position (row 5, rows 2/5/8/12). But in research data, we usually want to select rows by whether they meet a condition — “give me children who did X” rather than “give me row 7.”
This is where logical subsetting comes in. A logical condition like:

kids$mvpa_min >= 60

produces a vector of TRUE, FALSE, and possibly NA — one value per row. When you put that logical vector inside [, R keeps only the rows where the value is TRUE, and returns NA for rows where the condition itself was NA (this is different from using which(), which silently drops NAs instead — worth knowing when you’re not sure why your row counts don’t match).

Your turn
Find the children who get at least 60 minutes of MVPA. Return only id, age, mvpa_min, and vo2peak.

# Select children with at least 60 minutes of MVPA
# Keep only id, age, mvpa_min, and vo2peak

kids[
  kids$mvpa_min >= 60,
  c("id", "age", "mvpa_min", "vo2peak")
]



Try another one
Now find just the IDs of children who get less than 30 minutes of MVPA.

# Select the IDs of children with MVPA < 30

kids$id[kids$mvpa_min < 30]

Notice this time we’re subsetting a vector (kids$id), not the whole data frame — same logical-subsetting idea, just applied outside the data[rows, columns] pattern.

title: Subsetting in R Solutions
text:
Activity 4: Combining Conditions
Multiple logical conditions can be combined with:



Operator
Meaning




&
AND (both conditions must be TRUE)


|
OR (at least one condition must be TRUE)


!
NOT (flips TRUE/FALSE)



Always use the vectorized & and | here (not && / ||, which only compare a single value each and are meant for if statements).

kids$mvpa_min >= 60 &
  kids$bmi_z < 1


Your turn
Identify children who have either low physical activity (MVPA < 30 minutes) or high BMI z-score (≥ 2). Return id, age, bmi_z, mvpa_min.

# Select children with either:
#   MVPA < 30
#   OR BMI z-score >= 2
#
# Keep id, age, bmi_z, and mvpa_min

kids[
  kids$mvpa_min < 30 |
    kids$bmi_z >= 2,
  c("id", "age", "bmi_z", "mvpa_min")
]



Add another condition
Now restrict to girls who meet either of those criteria:

Female AND (low MVPA OR high BMI z-score)


# Select girls who either:
#   have MVPA < 30
#   OR have BMI z-score >= 2
#
# Keep id, age, sex, bmi_z, and mvpa_min

kids[
  kids$sex == "F" &
    (kids$mvpa_min < 30 | kids$bmi_z >= 2),
  c("id", "age", "sex", "bmi_z", "mvpa_min")
]

Why the parentheses matter: without them, R would evaluate & before | in a way that changes the meaning of the statement (operator precedence). The parentheses force the OR condition to be evaluated as a single unit before it’s combined with the AND. When in doubt, use parentheses to make your intent explicit — even when they’re not strictly required, they make code easier for you (and others) to read later.

title: Subsetting in R Solutions
text:
Activity 5: Putting It All Together
Your PI sends you this request:

“Can you give me the ID, age, sex, MVPA, BMI z-score, and systolic blood pressure for girls who either get less than 30 minutes of MVPA or have a BMI z-score of 2 or greater? Please exclude anyone with missing systolic blood pressure.”

Before writing any code, translate the request into pieces.
Which rows do we want?

Girls
AND either: MVPA < 30, OR BMI z-score ≥ 2
AND systolic BP is not missing

Which columns do we want?

id, age, sex, mvpa_min, bmi_z, sbp


Your turn

# Your code here

kids[
  kids$sex == "F" &
    (kids$mvpa_min < 30 | kids$bmi_z >= 2) &
    !is.na(kids$sbp),
  c(
    "id",
    "age",
    "sex",
    "mvpa_min",
    "bmi_z",
    "sbp"
  )
]

Notice !is.na(kids$sbp) — is.na() returns TRUE where a value is missing, so !is.na() flips that to TRUE where a value is not missing (i.e., where you want to keep the row).

title: Data Import Hands-on Practice
text:
Why this matters
A database can hold much more data than you want to load into memory. With dbplyr, familiar dplyr code is translated into SQL and run in the database. You should generally filter and summarize first, then use collect() only when the result is small enough to bring into R.

title: Data Import Hands-on Practice
text:
Setup
Run this code to create a temporary in-memory SQLite database containing Palmer Penguins:

library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")

copy_to(
  con,
  palmerpenguins::penguins,
  "penguins",
  temporary = FALSE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

title: Data Import Hands-on Practice
text:
Why this matters
A webpage is a hierarchical document, not a ready-made data frame. Web scraping often returns a list of possible elements, such as several HTML tables. You must inspect that list, select the relevant element, and then clean the resulting rectangular data.

title: Data Import Hands-on Practice
text:
Your task
Use this public webpage:

url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population_(United_Nations)"

Complete the following:

Read the page with read_html().
Extract every HTML table with html_elements("table").
Convert those elements to tibbles with html_table().
Determine how many tables were found.
Inspect the first table with glimpse().
Select the first four columns.
Clean the column names with janitor::clean_names().


library(rvest)

# Write your code here







Note



Websites can change. Never assume that the table you want will always remain in the same position. Inspect the scraped result before choosing an element.








TipFinish early



Use slice_head(n = 10) to display only the first ten rows, or calculate which rows have the largest reported population.

Activity 2: switch()
switch() is a cleaner way to write an if/else if chain when you’re matching one variable against a fixed set of known values — like a code.

switch(
  "B",
  A = "Sedentary",
  B = "Lightly active",
  C = "Moderately active",
  D = "Very active"
)

Compare this to what the equivalent if/else if chain would look like — switch() says the same thing with a lot less repetition.

  D = "Very active"

switch() can take an unnamed final argument as a default, for values that don’t match anything listed:

switch(
  "Z",

  B = "Lightly active",
  "Unknown code"
)

if/else makes a decision for a single value — it can’t take a vector.
switch() is a shortcut for matching one variable against a known list of codes, with an optional default.
for loops repeat a block of code once per element — this is how you scale a one-value decision (if/switch) up to a whole dataset.

title: Control Flow
text:
Activity 1: if / else if / else

Why control flow?
Subsetting (last workshop) answers “which rows meet a condition?” Control flow answers a different question: “given one value, which branch of logic should run?” This matters when the action you want to take is more complex than just keeping or dropping a row. e.g., assigning a category, printing a message, or triggering different calculations.
The basic shape:

# if (condition) {
# runs if condition is TRUE
#} else if (other_condition) {
# runs if condition is FALSE and other_condition is TRUE
#} else {
# runs if nothing above was TRUE
#}

A few things worth knowing:

if expects a single TRUE/FALSE — not a vector. Feeding it a vector of length > 1 will error (or has in recent R versions).
if/else returns a value, so you can assign the result directly: x <- if (a) 1 else 2.
This is different from ifelse(), which is vectorized and works element-by-element over a whole vector — useful later, but not what we’re practicing here.



Step 1: Classify one patient’s blood pressure
Standard categories (simplified for this exercise):

sbp < 120: “Normal”
sbp >= 120 & sbp < 130: “Elevated”
sbp >= 130 & sbp < 140: “High Stage 1”
sbp >= 140: “High Stage 2”


# Using patients$sbp[2], write an if / else if / else chain that prints the correct category



Step 2: Handle missing data
Patient 7 has a missing sbp value. Right now, running your code from Step 1 on patients$sbp[7] will likely throw an error or behave oddly, because if can’t evaluate NA as TRUE/FALSE.

# Add a check at the top of your if/else chain: if the value is NA,
# print "Missing" instead of evaluating the BP conditions

Why this matters for real data: any time you write if around a variable that might have missing values, you need to decide up front what should happen for NA — R won’t decide for you (it will error).

Activity 3: for loops
A for loop repeats the same block of code once per element of a sequence — useful when you want to apply an if/else decision (Activity 1) or a switch() (Activity 2) to every patient, not just one.

for (i in 1:5) {
  print(i)
}

title: Control Flow
Control Flow
text:
Activity 2: switch()
switch() is a cleaner way to write an if/else if chain when you’re matching one variable against a fixed set of known values, like a code.

switch(
  "B",
  A = "Sedentary",
  B = "Lightly active",
  C = "Moderately active",
  D = "Very active"
)

Compare this to what the equivalent if/else if chain would look like switch() says the same thing with a lot less repetition.

Step 1: Translate one code

# Use switch() to translate patients$activity_code[5] into its
# full label

switch(
  patients$activity_code[5],
  A = "Sedentary",
  B = "Lightly active",
  C = "Moderately active",
  D = "Very active"
)



Step 2: Add a fallback
switch() can take an unnamed final argument as a default, for values that don’t match anything listed:

switch(
  "Z",
  A = "Sedentary",
  B = "Lightly active",
  "Unknown code"
)


# Test your switch() from Step 1 on the value "Z" (a code that doesn't exist in our data) — add a default so it doesn't error

switch(
  "Z",
  A = "Sedentary",
  B = "Lightly active",
  C = "Moderately active",
  D = "Very active",
  "Unknown code"
)

title: Control Flow
Control Flow
text:
Key Takeaways

if/else makes a decision for a single value — it can’t take a vector.
switch() is a shortcut for matching one variable against a known list of codes, with an optional default.
for loops repeat a block of code once per element — this is how you scale a one-value decision (if/switch) up to a whole dataset.
next skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on — handy for skipping missing or bad data inside a loop.
Always ask: is this a single value (if/switch) or a whole vector/column at once (loop, or later: ifelse()/purrr::map())?

Tier 1: f_to_c()
Formula: C = (F - 32) * 5/9
Write a function called f_to_c() that converts a temperature in Fahrenheit to Celsius. Test it on 98.6 and 32.

Formula: miles = steps * 2.5 / 5280 (average stride length of 2.5 ft, 5,280 ft per mile)
Write a function called steps_to_miles() that converts a step count to miles, with a digits argument (defaulting to 1) that controls how many decimal places the result is rounded to. Test it on 8000 steps with the default rounding, and again with digits = 3.

title: Transform
text:
Run a Summary Table
Execute the code below to view a table summarizing the destination, temperature, wind speed, time in the air, and distance by Airline carrier. The gtsummary package is excellent for building tables in R for presentations or manuscripts. Converting to a flextable allows more control over formatting for creating publication-ready tables.

# Install the gtsummary package if not already installed
install.packages("gtsummary")

flights |>
  dplyr::select(carrier, dest, temp, wind_speed, air_time, distance) |>
  gtsummary::tbl_summary(
    by = carrier,
    missing = "no",
    statistic = gtsummary::all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ± {sd}",
    type = distance ~ "continuous",
    label = list(
      dest ~ "Destination",
      temp ~ "Temperature",
      wind_speed ~ "Wind Speed",
      air_time ~ "Time in the Air",
      distance ~ "Distance"
    )
  ) |>
  gtsummary::as_flex_table()
